alt: Article 2.1, a limited right with no derogation except for deaths from lawful acts of war, produces four duties: the negative duty not to take life (McCann v UK), the positive framework duty to have effective criminal law and regulation (Öneryildiz v Turkey), the positive operational duty to protect people at real and immediate risk (Osman v UK), and the procedural duty to investigate (Jordan v UK).
caption: Do not kill, protect life through laws and action, and investigate deaths.

alt: The Osman test in five parts: the authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual from a third party’s criminal acts, and failed to take reasonable measures. Applied: Osman v UK, test not met; Edwards v UK, breach; Van Colle, no breach; Rabone, breach.
caption: The operational duty is demanding: the risk must be real, immediate and known.

alt: Three cases along a line from the start to the end of life. Vo v France: the Court declined to decide whether an unborn child is a person, leaving it to the margin of appreciation. Evans v UK: no breach when embryos were to be destroyed. Pretty v UK: Article 2 gives no right to die, so the assisted suicide ban did not breach it.
caption: Article 2 leaves unborn life to the state and gives no right to die.

alt: Three questions for lethal force: was it for an aim in Article 2.2 (a) defence from unlawful violence, (b) lawful arrest or preventing escape, (c) quelling a riot; was it no more than absolutely necessary, a stricter test judged on honest belief for good reasons (Da Silva); and was the operation planned to minimise risk (McCann). Below, Stewart v UK found no breach in a riot, Güleç v Turkey found a breach.
caption: A listed aim, absolute necessity and careful planning: all three are needed.

alt: McCann v UK: soldiers shot three IRA suspects in Gibraltar. The soldiers themselves did not breach Article 2 because they honestly believed a bomb could be detonated remotely. The violation came from planning and control: no earlier arrest, no allowance for wrong intelligence, and training to shoot to kill.
caption: Even where the shooter is not at fault, poor planning can breach Article 2.

alt: Five features of an effective investigation from Jordan v UK: independent, capable of establishing the facts and identifying those responsible, prompt, open to public scrutiny, and involving the family of the deceased. Failing these can breach Article 2 on its own.
caption: The duty to investigate can be breached on its own.

alt: Marek’s case in five steps: identify the aim under Article 2.2 (a) or (b); the officer’s honest belief may justify the shot (Da Silva); letting him enter the bank may breach Article 2 through poor planning (McCann); the investigation was not independent and excluded the family (Jordan); so a likely violation on planning and investigation.
caption: The shot may be justified while the planning and investigation still breach Article 2.
